raw_evidence.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
raw_evidence.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. His season rank in the NBA went from #8 at the peak to #153 in a typical year.

raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 22 wins in 2005, rank 1,338 by 2008
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis's career timeline is the most compressed fall in the dataset among well-known players. He entered the majors in 2003 with a 3.4-WAR rookie year (rank 104 in MLB) and won NL Rookie of the Year. His 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, 6.5 WAR — was the 8th-best year by any player in baseball that year and produced a runner-up Cy Young finish. His next five seasons: WAR of 3.0, 0.9, -0.7, -0.2, -0.2, with league ranks of 127, 370, 1,338, 1,123, 1,085. By 2008, his rank was essentially 'last meaningful player in MLB.' He was out of the majors for good by 2012. The shape is a single thin spike surrounded by a long decline into replacement-level production.

raw_evidence.label: The Pudding's 2018 one-hit wonders article
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's April 2018 article 'One-Hit Wonders in Sports' by Russell Goldenberg and Jan Diehm. The piece asks a deceptively simple question: which professional athletes had exactly one great year, then disappeared? The authors looked at eight pro leagues over thirty years (1988–2017), ranked every player each season by a sport-appropriate statistic, and defined a 'one-hit wonder' as a player who finished in the top 20 exactly once and never came within striking distance (top 50) in any other season of their career. The result is both a statistical exercise in outliers and a human story about careers that never made it back.

raw_evidence.label: What the ranking stat is for each sport
raw_evidence.content: Each league uses a different single-number catch-all that approximates overall value. Basketball (NBA and WNBA) uses VORP — Value Over Replacement Player — a box-score estimate of a player's points above what a league-minimum replacement would produce. Baseball (MLB) uses WAR (Wins Above Replacement), hockey (NHL) uses point shares, tennis (ATP and WTA) uses year-end ranking points, and golf (PGA and LPGA) uses money earned on tour. These stats were chosen because they are the closest thing to apples-to-apples 'who was most valuable this season' within each sport, and because they have reasonably complete historical coverage back to the late 1980s. A consequence: 'top 20' means something slightly different sport-to-sport, but within a sport a top-20 season is unambiguously elite.

raw_evidence.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
raw_evidence.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

raw_evidence.label: The Pudding's 2018 one-hit wonders article
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's April 2018 article 'One-Hit Wonders in Sports' by Russell Goldenberg and Jan Diehm. The piece asks a deceptively simple question: which professional athletes had exactly one great year, then disappeared? The authors looked at eight pro leagues over thirty years (1988–2017), ranked every player each season by a sport-appropriate statistic, and defined a 'one-hit wonder' as a player who finished in the top 20 exactly once and never came within striking distance (top 50) in any other season of their career. The result is both a statistical exercise in outliers and a human story about careers that never made it back.

raw_evidence.label: What the ranking stat is for each sport
raw_evidence.content: Each league uses a different single-number catch-all that approximates overall value. Basketball (NBA and WNBA) uses VORP — Value Over Replacement Player — a box-score estimate of a player's points above what a league-minimum replacement would produce. Baseball (MLB) uses WAR (Wins Above Replacement), hockey (NHL) uses point shares, tennis (ATP and WTA) uses year-end ranking points, and golf (PGA and LPGA) uses money earned on tour. These stats were chosen because they are the closest thing to apples-to-apples 'who was most valuable this season' within each sport, and because they have reasonably complete historical coverage back to the late 1980s. A consequence: 'top 20' means something slightly different sport-to-sport, but within a sport a top-20 season is unambiguously elite.

raw_evidence.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
raw_evidence.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

raw_evidence.content: Applying the Pudding's definition — at least 5 seasons played, exactly one top-20 finish, and never any other top-50 finish — identifies 78 one-hit wonders out of 1,076 eligible careers in the dataset. Put differently: most professional athletes who ever cracked the top 20 of their league did it more than once (93%), but a meaningful minority had their single great season and never came close again.

raw_evidence.label: The Pudding's 2018 one-hit wonders article
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's April 2018 article 'One-Hit Wonders in Sports' by Russell Goldenberg and Jan Diehm. The piece asks a deceptively simple question: which professional athletes had exactly one great year, then disappeared? The authors looked at eight pro leagues over thirty years (1988–2017), ranked every player each season by a sport-appropriate statistic, and defined a 'one-hit wonder' as a player who finished in the top 20 exactly once and never came within striking distance (top 50) in any other season of their career. The result is both a statistical exercise in outliers and a human story about careers that never made it back.

raw_evidence.label: What the ranking stat is for each sport
raw_evidence.content: Each league uses a different single-number catch-all that approximates overall value. Basketball (NBA and WNBA) uses VORP — Value Over Replacement Player — a box-score estimate of a player's points above what a league-minimum replacement would produce. Baseball (MLB) uses WAR (Wins Above Replacement), hockey (NHL) uses point shares, tennis (ATP and WTA) uses year-end ranking points, and golf (PGA and LPGA) uses money earned on tour. These stats were chosen because they are the closest thing to apples-to-apples 'who was most valuable this season' within each sport, and because they have reasonably complete historical coverage back to the late 1980s. A consequence: 'top 20' means something slightly different sport-to-sport, but within a sport a top-20 season is unambiguously elite.

raw_evidence.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
raw_evidence.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

raw_evidence.label: 78 players out of 1,076 eligible meet the strict one-hit wonder definition — 7.2%
raw_evidence.content: Applying the Pudding's definition — at least 5 seasons played, exactly one top-20 finish, and never any other top-50 finish — identifies 78 one-hit wonders out of 1,076 eligible careers in the dataset. That is 7.2% overall, or roughly one in every fourteen elite careers. Put differently: most professional athletes who ever cracked the top 20 of their league did it more than once (93%), but a meaningful minority had their single great season and never came close again.

raw_evidence.label: Baseball is the one-hit wonder capital, the WNBA the opposite
raw_evidence.content: The share of one-hit wonders varies enormously by league. MLB leads, with 32 of 206 eligible players (15.5%) fitting the definition — more than one in seven big-league careers. NHL follows at 13.0% (21 of 162) and PGA at 10.0% (11 of 110). The women's leagues and the NBA sit at the other end: just 3.0% of LPGA careers (4 of 132), 3.0% of NBA careers (4 of 133), and a single WNBA player (Tracy Reid) in 120 careers (0.8%). The pattern suggests that leagues with deeper talent pools and higher year-to-year noise in the ranking metric (baseball WAR, hockey point shares) produce more extreme outliers than leagues with more compressed, predictable tops (WNBA, NBA, women's tennis).

raw_evidence.label: The Pudding's 2018 one-hit wonders article
raw_evidence.content: This dataset accompanies The Pudding's April 2018 article 'One-Hit Wonders in Sports' by Russell Goldenberg and Jan Diehm. The piece asks a deceptively simple question: which professional athletes had exactly one great year, then disappeared? The authors looked at eight pro leagues over thirty years (1988–2017), ranked every player each season by a sport-appropriate statistic, and defined a 'one-hit wonder' as a player who finished in the top 20 exactly once and never came within striking distance (top 50) in any other season of their career. The result is both a statistical exercise in outliers and a human story about careers that never made it back.

raw_evidence.label: Most peaks happen years 4-6 of career, not rookie year
raw_evidence.content: The career-timing of the peak season is more spread out than the 'rookie sensation' archetype suggests. Of 78 one-hit wonders, only 9 (12%) peaked in their first year, 16 (21%) in years 2-3, 25 (32%) in years 4-6, 21 (27%) in years 7-10, and 7 (9%) in year 11 or later. The median peak is at career-year 5, with a standard deviation of 3.4 years. This means the stereotype of the flash-in-the-pan rookie (think Dontrelle Willis) is one mode, but the more common mode is a veteran who has a career year mid-career (Dana Barros peaked in his 6th season; Rich Beem in his 5th). Late-career peaks also exist — 7 players had their peak after year 11, the most extreme being Omar Vizquel's 1999 season (year 11) at rank 17.

The median peak is at career-year 5, with a standard deviation of 3.4 years. raw_evidence.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
raw_evidence.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

Baseball and hockey produce the steepest immediate declines because the metric is single-season-noisy; tennis and golf, where rank points and money accumulate over many tournaments, show smaller one-year drops but longer tails. The median one-hit wonder was essentially not the same player the very next season.

raw_evidence.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
raw_evidence.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

raw_evidence.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
raw_evidence.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. His season rank in the NBA went from #8 at the peak to #153 in a typical year.

raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

raw_evidence.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
raw_evidence.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

raw_evidence.label: Jiri Hudler: the NHL pick
raw_evidence.content: Jiri Hudler, a Czech winger who spent most of his career as a secondary scorer for Detroit and then Calgary, had one All-Star, Lady Byng-winning season in 2014–15 — 31 goals, 76 points, and a 13th-place finish in NHL point shares. His median career rank was 220. By 2017–18 he could not secure an NHL contract and soon retired. The NHL's deep roster talent and the role-player structure of the sport make hockey a particularly interesting one-hit-wonder case: Hudler was a legitimately good NHL player for a decade, but one season he was elite, and that year is a striking spike on his career timeline.

raw_evidence.label: Women's leagues: WNBA, LPGA, WTA selections
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding highlighted three women's-league one-hit wonders. Tracy Reid won 1998 WNBA Rookie of the Year with the Charlotte Sting, averaging 16.7 PPG, and her rank fell outside the top 100 the very next season. Hilary Lunke won the 2003 U.S. Women's Open in a Monday playoff — her only LPGA win — and never again finished in the LPGA money-list top 30. Karolina Sprem reached the 2004 Wimbledon quarterfinals and the WTA top 20, then spent the rest of her career outside the top 50 before retiring in 2008. Including women's leagues is important: career-arc volatility is driven by talent-pool size and structural support (prize money, development pipelines), both of which differ between the men's and women's tours.

raw_evidence.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
raw_evidence.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. His season rank in the NBA went from #8 at the peak to #153 in a typical year.

raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

raw_evidence.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
raw_evidence.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

His median career rank was 220. By 2017–18 he could not secure an NHL contract and soon retired. The NHL's deep roster talent and the role-player structure of the sport make hockey a particularly interesting one-hit-wonder case: Hudler was a legitimately good NHL player for a decade, but one season he was elite, and that year is a striking spike on his career timeline.

raw_evidence.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
raw_evidence.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. His season rank in the NBA went from #8 at the peak to #153 in a typical year.

raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

raw_evidence.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
raw_evidence.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

raw_evidence.label: Jiri Hudler: the NHL pick
raw_evidence.content: Jiri Hudler, a Czech winger who spent most of his career as a secondary scorer for Detroit and then Calgary, had one All-Star, Lady Byng-winning season in 2014–15 — 31 goals, 76 points, and a 13th-place finish in NHL point shares. His median career rank was 220. By 2017–18 he could not secure an NHL contract and soon retired. The NHL's deep roster talent and the role-player structure of the sport make hockey a particularly interesting one-hit-wonder case: Hudler was a legitimately good NHL player for a decade, but one season he was elite, and that year is a striking spike on his career timeline.

raw_evidence.label: Women's leagues: WNBA, LPGA, WTA selections
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding highlighted three women's-league one-hit wonders. Tracy Reid won 1998 WNBA Rookie of the Year with the Charlotte Sting, averaging 16.7 PPG, and her rank fell outside the top 100 the very next season. Hilary Lunke won the 2003 U.S. Women's Open in a Monday playoff — her only LPGA win — and never again finished in the LPGA money-list top 30. Karolina Sprem reached the 2004 Wimbledon quarterfinals and the WTA top 20, then spent the rest of her career outside the top 50 before retiring in 2008. Including women's leagues is important: career-arc volatility is driven by talent-pool size and structural support (prize money, development pipelines), both of which differ between the men's and women's tours.

raw_evidence.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
raw_evidence.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

raw_evidence.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
raw_evidence.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

raw_evidence.label: Jiri Hudler: the NHL pick

His median career rank was 220. By 2017–18 he could not secure an NHL contract and soon retired. The NHL's deep roster talent and the role-player structure of the sport make hockey a particularly interesting one-hit-wonder case: Hudler was a legitimately good NHL player for a decade, but one season he was elite, and that year is a striking spike on his career timeline.

raw_evidence.label: Women's leagues: WNBA, LPGA, WTA selections

raw_evidence.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
raw_evidence.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. His season rank in the NBA went from #8 at the peak to #153 in a typical year.

raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

raw_evidence.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
raw_evidence.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

raw_evidence.label: Jiri Hudler: the NHL pick
raw_evidence.content: Jiri Hudler, a Czech winger who spent most of his career as a secondary scorer for Detroit and then Calgary, had one All-Star, Lady Byng-winning season in 2014–15 — 31 goals, 76 points, and a 13th-place finish in NHL point shares. His median career rank was 220. By 2017–18 he could not secure an NHL contract and soon retired. The NHL's deep roster talent and the role-player structure of the sport make hockey a particularly interesting one-hit-wonder case: Hudler was a legitimately good NHL player for a decade, but one season he was elite, and that year is a striking spike on his career timeline.

raw_evidence.label: Women's leagues: WNBA, LPGA, WTA selections
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding highlighted three women's-league one-hit wonders. Tracy Reid won 1998 WNBA Rookie of the Year with the Charlotte Sting, averaging 16.7 PPG, and her rank fell outside the top 100 the very next season. Hilary Lunke won the 2003 U.S. Women's Open in a Monday playoff — her only LPGA win — and never again finished in the LPGA money-list top 30. Karolina Sprem reached the 2004 Wimbledon quarterfinals and the WTA top 20, then spent the rest of her career outside the top 50 before retiring in 2008. Including women's leagues is important: career-arc volatility is driven by talent-pool size and structural support (prize money, development pipelines), both of which differ between the men's and women's tours.

raw_evidence.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
raw_evidence.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

raw_evidence.label: Dana Barros: the canonical NBA one-hit wonder
raw_evidence.content: The poster child for the NBA in The Pudding's analysis is Dana Barros. In 1994–95, his second season with the Philadelphia 76ers, Barros averaged 20.6 points, 7.5 assists, and shot 46% from three over all 82 games. He won Most Improved Player, was voted an All-Star, and dropped a 50-point, 8-rebound night against the Houston Rockets. He also set an NBA record by hitting at least one three-pointer in 89 consecutive games. It was the only year of his 14-season career that he averaged even 14 points per game: his career average ended up at 10.5 PPG. Philadelphia could not keep him — Boston signed him to a big contract as a free agent — and his role immediately collapsed back to that of a rotational guard. His season rank in the NBA went from #8 at the peak to #153 in a typical year.

raw_evidence.label: Dontrelle Willis: 'D-Train' and the collapse
raw_evidence.content: Dontrelle Willis won NL Rookie of the Year for the 2003 Florida Marlins and helped them win the World Series, but it was his 2005 season — 22 wins, 2.63 ERA, five shutouts, the most wins in baseball — that made him the MLB's definitive one-hit wonder. He finished 2nd in Cy Young voting behind Chris Carpenter. The decline was swift and medically documented: after a trade to Detroit and the onset of what he later described as severe anxiety disorder, his control evaporated. His WAR went 6.5, 3.0, 0.9, and his rank tumbled from 8th in MLB to roughly 370th by the end of his career. Willis's story is the regression-to-the-mean chart reshaped by injury, mental health, and the specific pressure of being a 23-year-old face of a franchise.

raw_evidence.label: Rich Beem: the PGA's unlikely major winner
raw_evidence.content: Rich Beem sold car stereos and worked in a pro shop before his professional golf career took off. In August 2002 he won The International, then two weeks later won the PGA Championship at Hazeltine by holding off a charging Tiger Woods — Woods birdied his last four holes and still lost by one stroke. Beem briefly rose to #7 in the world. Within two years he was outside the top 180. In money-list terms he finished 4th on tour in 2002 and never again cracked the top 100. He is the perfect illustration of how a single four-day hot streak at one major can reshape a season's earnings and rank without reshaping the underlying golfer.

raw_evidence.label: Jiri Hudler: the NHL pick
raw_evidence.content: Jiri Hudler, a Czech winger who spent most of his career as a secondary scorer for Detroit and then Calgary, had one All-Star, Lady Byng-winning season in 2014–15 — 31 goals, 76 points, and a 13th-place finish in NHL point shares. His median career rank was 220. By 2017–18 he could not secure an NHL contract and soon retired. The NHL's deep roster talent and the role-player structure of the sport make hockey a particularly interesting one-hit-wonder case: Hudler was a legitimately good NHL player for a decade, but one season he was elite, and that year is a striking spike on his career timeline.

raw_evidence.label: Women's leagues: WNBA, LPGA, WTA selections
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding highlighted three women's-league one-hit wonders. Tracy Reid won 1998 WNBA Rookie of the Year with the Charlotte Sting, averaging 16.7 PPG, and her rank fell outside the top 100 the very next season. Hilary Lunke won the 2003 U.S. Women's Open in a Monday playoff — her only LPGA win — and never again finished in the LPGA money-list top 30. Karolina Sprem reached the 2004 Wimbledon quarterfinals and the WTA top 20, then spent the rest of her career outside the top 50 before retiring in 2008. Including women's leagues is important: career-arc volatility is driven by talent-pool size and structural support (prize money, development pipelines), both of which differ between the men's and women's tours.

raw_evidence.label: What the ranking stat is for each sport
raw_evidence.content: Each league uses a different single-number catch-all that approximates overall value. Basketball (NBA and WNBA) uses VORP — Value Over Replacement Player — a box-score estimate of a player's points above what a league-minimum replacement would produce. Baseball (MLB) uses WAR (Wins Above Replacement), hockey (NHL) uses point shares, tennis (ATP and WTA) uses year-end ranking points, and golf (PGA and LPGA) uses money earned on tour. These stats were chosen because they are the closest thing to apples-to-apples 'who was most valuable this season' within each sport, and because they have reasonably complete historical coverage back to the late 1980s. A consequence: 'top 20' means something slightly different sport-to-sport, but within a sport a top-20 season is unambiguously elite.

raw_evidence.label: The 15 most extreme one-hit wonders — MLB dominates the tail
raw_evidence.content: When ranked by the absolute size of the gap between peak and median rank, baseball dominates the extreme tail. The single largest gap belongs to Andres Torres (2010 SF Giants): rank 10 at peak, median career rank 848 — an 838-place gap. Next are Dave Hollins (19 → 719) and Carlos Pena (17 → 481), both MLB. Only two non-MLB players crack the top 10: Joachim Johansson (ATP, 2004 peak 11 → median 377) and Pascal Dupuis (NHL, 2013 peak 17 → median 376). Dontrelle Willis and Franklin Gutierrez also appear in the top 10. The pattern reinforces the league-level finding: sports with larger eligible populations and more volatility in single-number metrics generate the most extreme individual outliers.

raw_evidence.label: Why readers care: the myth of sustained excellence
raw_evidence.content: The reason this topic has audience pull beyond sports fandom is that it speaks to a broader intuition people carry about careers and success: that one great performance proves you belong, and you should be able to repeat it. The data say otherwise. Sustained excellence is rare; one-year breakouts without follow-up are not. That tension — between the narrative of 'you made it' and the statistics of 'most don't stay' — is what makes the one-hit wonder a perennial sports-writing topic. The Pudding's contribution is quantifying how many of these careers actually exist across three decades of pro sports, and naming them.

raw_evidence.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
raw_evidence.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

raw_evidence.label: Why this is harder than it sounds: regression to the mean
raw_evidence.content: Statisticians have a phrase for what makes a one-hit wonder story a one-hit wonder story: regression to the mean. When any measurement involves a mix of skill and luck — and a single sports season always does — the most extreme results in one year are disproportionately driven by lucky bounces, favorable matchups, or anomalously hot streaks. Next season, the skill remains but the luck resets, and the extreme outlier tends to drift back toward the crowd. In sports this is so common it has its own name, the 'sophomore slump,' and it produces the famous 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx': teams and players on the cover performed well enough to earn the spot, then performed more normally afterward. What The Pudding's dataset isolates is the extreme tail of this phenomenon: athletes whose one great year was so far above their baseline that they never again came close. These are not just sophomore slumps — they are careers where one season looks like a rounding error in the time series.

raw_evidence.label: Why readers care: the myth of sustained excellence
raw_evidence.content: The reason this topic has audience pull beyond sports fandom is that it speaks to a broader intuition people carry about careers and success: that one great performance proves you belong, and you should be able to repeat it. The data say otherwise. Sustained excellence is rare; one-year breakouts without follow-up are not. That tension — between the narrative of 'you made it' and the statistics of 'most don't stay' — is what makes the one-hit wonder a perennial sports-writing topic. The Pudding's contribution is quantifying how many of these careers actually exist across three decades of pro sports, and naming them.

raw_evidence.label: The median one-hit wonder was a 20-place star — everyone else was 150-400
raw_evidence.content: Across all 78 one-hit wonders, the median peak rank is 15 and the median career rank is roughly 200. That gap — 185 places between their best year and their typical year — is the statistical signature of the phenomenon. MLB one-hit wonders have the most extreme spike: their median peak is around rank 16 but their median career rank is 271 — a 22.9x multiplier, meaning their typical season was 22 times worse in rank terms than their best season. LPGA sits at the other end: 6.4x spike, because the LPGA field tracked in the data is smaller and one-hit wonders didn't fall as far before disappearing.
raw_evidence.code:
agg = ohw_df.groupby('league').agg(
    n=('id','size'),
    median_spike=('spike_ratio','median'),
    median_gap=('gap','median'),
    worst_drop=('worst_rank','max'),
).round(1)
print(agg)
print()
